references.text: Habakkuk prophesies that the stones in the wall will cry out – an image reminiscent of Jesus' words that the stones will cry out if the disciples remain silent ([ref:Hab 2:11|Habakkuk 2:11]).

Psalm 148 calls all creation to praise the Lord, including lifeless things. Jesus' point is that God's praise cannot be held back – if people do not praise him, creation itself will ([ref:Sal 148:1-4|Psalms 148:1-4]).

The stone motif in the Psalms – the stone rejected by the builders – emphasizes that God can use what humans reject, just as the stones in Jesus' words represent God's inevitable praise ([ref:Sal 118:22-23|Psalms 118:22-23]).

The immediate context: The disciples are praising God with a loud voice, and the Pharisees ask Jesus to rebuke them. Jesus' answer in verse 40 is a direct response to the Pharisees' objection ([ref:Luk 19:37-39|Luke 19:37-39]).

In Matthew, Jesus defends the children's praise in the temple with a quote from the Psalms – God has prepared praise from the mouths of children and infants. In the same way, he defends his disciples' praise in Luke 19:40 ([ref:Matt 21:15-16|Matthew 21:15-16]).

John the Baptist says that God can raise up children for Abraham from the stones – a related motif where the stones represent God's sovereign power to act independently of human will ([ref:Matt 3:9|Matthew 3:9]).

All creation – heaven, earth, sea, and trees – is called to rejoice before the Lord. This cosmic praise supports Jesus' words that creation itself will testify about him if people remain silent ([ref:Sal 96:11-13|Psalms 96:11-13]).

Joshua says that a stone shall be a witness, because it has heard all the Lord's words. Stones as witnesses are a biblical motif that provides background for Jesus' statement that the stones will cry out ([ref:Jos 24:27|Joshua 24:27]).

Isaiah describes mountains and hills breaking into shouts of joy, and trees clapping their hands – creation's praise cannot be held back, which provides background for Jesus' words ([ref:Jes 55:12|Isaiah 55:12]).
